questions.prompt: Why is there no meaningful security distinction between WriteDacl and GenericAll?
options: They apply to different object types entirely
WriteDacl lets the holder rewrite the object's ACL and grant themselves GenericAll -- a one-step path
GenericAll is a subset of WriteDacl
Neither right actually permits any change
questions.explanation: WriteDacl (and WriteOwner) each convert into full control in a single step, so treating them as lesser permissions in an access review is a mistake.

questions.prompt: Why do traditional access reviews structurally miss ACL-based escalation paths?
options: Because ACLs are encrypted and unreadable
Because each individual grant looks defensible in isolation -- the path only exists when you traverse the whole chain of grants and nested groups
Because access reviews are performed too frequently
Because ACLs are not stored in Active Directory
questions.explanation: Each link in the chain was typically granted for a real reason, at a different time, by a different person. Only graph traversal across all of them reveals the path, which is why tooling like BloodHound exists.

A service account with an expired password
questions.explanation: Shadow admins pass membership-based reviews cleanly because their power comes from permissions rather than group membership -- and permissions are what most reviews never enumerate.

questions.prompt: Why is servicePrincipalName being written onto an account by another principal a red flag?
options: It prevents the account from logging in
It converts GenericWrite over that account into a Kerberoasting opportunity
It automatically grants Domain Admin rights
It disables Kerberos for the whole domain
questions.explanation: Adding an SPN to an account makes it Kerberoastable, so an attacker with GenericWrite can create the conditions for offline credential cracking against an account that previously had no SPN.
